His flaw is the bouncer's wariness worn into the bone: he reads everyone as a potential problem first, and it takes real consistency to move from 'managed' to 'trusted'.

quest.title: The gut thing at the door
quest.hook: Endō's low-sensitivity reads trouble before it arrives — and his door is a gate to the Roppongi night.
stages: Behave at his door long enough to move from managed to known.
Earn the safe passage he grants the people he trusts.
At full trust he becomes an early-warning net for the nightlife wards.
quest.payoff: Safe passage and a sensor across Roppongi's doors — the night's own alarm system, tuned to Rei's kind of trouble.

goto_hideki.cap: A soundproof room and a blind eye. For a price. Everything here has one.
goto_hideki.meta: Gotō Hideki · floor manager, Tamaya Hall
back: Forty-seven, floor manager at Tamaya Hall in Kabukichō, and a man who has made a comfortable career out of selling discretion to people who need a room with no memory. Gotō is cash-and-carry silence: a soundproof space, a blind eye, a meeting that never happened, all available for the right consideration and all equally for sale to the next buyer. He answers, uneasily, to people above him, and that chain of obligation is the hook in him.

For Rei he is a transactional door — useful, unreliable, and dangerous in proportion to how much Rei relies on him. At his best he lets slip who he answers to, a hook into the organised underside of the district; at his worst he sells Rei's meeting to whoever pays more, because loyalty was never part of the price. He is not cruel, just entirely commercial.
His flaw is that he's in over his head with the people above him and will trade anyone's safety, including his own customers', to stay in their good graces.

quest.title: Cash-and-carry silence
quest.hook: Gotō sells discretion to anyone — and might let slip who he answers to, if the price is right.
stages: Pay his price for a room and a blind eye, knowing it's for sale twice.
Get him talking about the chain of obligation above him.
At depth he lets slip who he answers to — a hook into the organised underside.
quest.payoff: A purchasable safe room and a thread into the district's organised crime — never trust it not to be sold back.

saeki_reno.cap: My clubs, my floors, my eyes. Make it worth my while and they're yours too.
back: Forty-nine, owner of Vault and two other clubs, and a man who sits atop a small empire of nightlife real estate that doubles, for the right partner, as the best surveillance grid in the district. Saeki is a businessman first and last — affable, calculating, allergic to anything that costs him without returning more — but the clubs he owns see everything the night does, and that makes him a uniquely valuable ally to someone who needs doors, eyes, and a safe room above the floor.

For Rei he is a base waiting to be unlocked: at full trust, his clubs open as a headquarters — doors, eyes, a safe room above Vault, and all of nightlife's intelligence flowing up to one desk. He gives it only when convinced Rei is an asset rather than a liability, because Saeki does nothing that doesn't pencil out. Endō works his door, which means earning Saeki and earning Endō braid together.
His flaw is that his loyalty is exactly as long as his profit; the moment Rei costs more than he returns, the affable host becomes Gotō's kind of problem.

quest.title: The clubs as a base
quest.hook: Saeki's nightlife empire is the district's best surveillance grid — open to a partner who pencils out.
stages: Prove you're an asset, not a liability; he runs the numbers on everyone.
Earn a word with Endō and the run of his floors.
At full trust the clubs open as a base — doors, eyes, a safe room, the night's intel.
quest.payoff: A nightlife headquarters and surveillance grid across the district — for exactly as long as Rei keeps penciling out.

miyamoto_kazuo.cap: The shrine has stood two hundred years. It remembers what the Directorate forgets.
back: Sixty-six, head priest of a Shinto shrine that has kept its corner of the city for two centuries, and a shrine-line practitioner whose tradition predates and quietly outperforms the CVD's secular instruments. Miyamoto does not think in registers and grades; he thinks in kami, purity, and the slow neighbourly work of keeping the boundary between worlds in good repair. He has cleansed more thin spots than any licensed operative, and never filed a single one.

For Rei he is the door to a method the bureau cannot replicate: at full trust he teaches the shrine's wards or sets them himself by a two-hundred-year discipline, and offers cleansings, charms, and the kind of counsel that comes from a man who has watched the boundary breathe for forty years. He gives it on respect, not on rank — disrespect the shrine and the courtesy ends.
His shrine cat keeps the grounds with him, fed at the offering box and treated as staff; the old priest swears it notices a thin spot opening before he does.

quest.title: The shrine's two-hundred-year ward
quest.hook: Miyamoto wards and cleanses by a tradition the CVD can't reproduce — given on respect, never rank.
stages: Approach the shrine with respect, not as an operative working a source.
Earn a cleansing, a charm, honest counsel.
At full trust he teaches the ward methodology or sets it himself for a site.
quest.payoff: A spiritual method outside the bureau's reach — wards and cleansings the institution literally cannot do.

companion.name: Mike
companion.desc: A three-coloured shrine cat that has decided it is clergy. It patrols the grounds, accepts offerings as tribute, and grows still and watchful at the exact spots Miyamoto later finds need cleansing.
companion.role: Thin-spot sense: stares and bristles where the boundary is wearing, an early reading the old priest has learned to trust.

rev_egami_jaku.cap: There is exorcism, and there is what the Directorate calls exorcism. They are not the same act.
back: Fifty-nine, a Shingon temple priest and esoteric ritualist whose tradition holds methods of genuine exorcism that the CVD's containment-and-suppression doctrine cannot replicate. Egami is grave, exacting, and unsentimental about the cost: a true esoteric exorcism is not a procedure, it is a transaction with the unseen that takes something real from the one who performs it. He does not do it lightly, and he does not do it for institutions.

For Rei he is a last resort with teeth: at full trust he will perform a true Shingon exorcism — a method the bureau cannot replicate, at real cost to himself — for a cause he judges worthy. Short of that he offers counsel, a warding, an esoteric text translated. He weighs the asker as carefully as the asking, and declines, gently, to be anyone's weapon.
His flaw, if it is one, is the ascetic's distance: he has given so much to the work that ordinary human need can read to him as noise, and Rei has to prove the cause is real, not merely urgent.

quest.title: What the Directorate cannot replicate
quest.hook: Egami holds a true esoteric exorcism the CVD can't reproduce — performed only for a cause he judges worthy, at real cost.
stages: Earn a grave priest's grave courtesy.
Prove the cause is worthy, not just urgent; he refuses to be a weapon.
At full trust he performs the Shingon exorcism, paying its real cost.
quest.payoff: A method of genuine exorcism beyond the bureau's doctrine — the spiritual heavy artillery, given once and dearly.

father_anselm_mbeki.cap: Rome has its rite. I have my conscience. When they disagree, the conscience wins.
back: Sixty-one, a Catholic priest and trained Roman-rite exorcist far from the diocese that ordained him, ministering to a diaspora congregation in a city that has its own older spirits. Father Anselm carries the full apparatus of Church exorcism and, more dangerously for the institutions, a conscience that will override both Rome and the CVD when a person needs sheltering more than a procedure needs following. He has hidden people the bureau wanted; he would do it again.

For Rei he is faith made practical: counsel, belief, a safe pew, and — at full trust — the rite itself, or shelter for someone the CVD means to disappear, performed on his own faith and judgement rather than anyone's permission. He is warm, stubborn, and entirely unintimidated by authority, having long since decided which authority he answers to.
His flaw is the moral certainty that makes him brave: he will shelter the wrong person as readily as the right one if his conscience is moved, and conscience is not always informed.

quest.title: Conscience over the rite
quest.hook: Father Anselm will perform the Roman rite — or hide someone the CVD wants — on his own judgement, not anyone's leave.
stages: Earn a priest's kindness and trust.
Show him a cause his conscience can stand behind.
At full trust he performs the rite, or shelters someone the bureau means to erase.
quest.payoff: A Roman-rite exorcist and a safe house that answers to conscience, not the CVD — sanctuary the institution can't override.

master_lin_wei.cap: Buy incense first. Then we talk. The respect is not optional; it is the method.
master_lin_wei.meta: Master Lin Wei · Taoist temple master
back: Sixty-three, master of a small Taoist temple and a fú-talisman ritualist whose craft reads the other side through a cosmology the CVD has no column for. Lin Wei is precise, prickly, and uninterested in being convenient; the respect his tradition demands is not ceremony for its own sake but part of how the work functions — disrespect the temple and the talismans simply do not take. He has drawn fú against things the bureau filed as unkillable.

For Rei he offers incense, a talisman, blunt advice, and — at full trust — a true fú drawn for one specific entity, plus the teaching of how his tradition reads the other side, a literacy no CVD manual contains. He gives it in order and on terms: buy incense first, earn the conversation, then perhaps the craft. He is generous underneath the prickliness, to those who approach correctly.
His flaw is exactly his strength worn too hard: the insistence on respect can tip into testing people who have already earned it, just to see the form kept.

quest.title: A true fú for one entity
quest.hook: Lin Wei draws talismans that work on what the bureau calls unkillable — for those who keep the form.
stages: Buy incense; keep the respect his method requires.
Earn the conversation, then the blunt advice.
At full trust he draws a true fú for a specific entity and teaches how his tradition reads the other side.
quest.payoff: Talismanic weapons calibrated to a specific entity, and a cosmology of reading the unseen the CVD doesn't have.

pak_sun_ja.cap: The dead are not gone, only unquiet. I can ask them. Sometimes they answer.
back: Fifty-five, a Korean shaman — a mudang — whose gut rites do something the CVD's instruments cannot: speak with the dead, reach a specific departed soul, or send a restless one on its way. Pak carries a tradition of genuine spirit-work in a city that pretends the dead stay put, and she has spent a lifetime being the person families come to when the official answers run out. Fierce, warm, and without patience for the disrespectful.

For Rei she is access to the dead themselves: at full trust she performs a gut for his case — reaching a specific dead person, or guiding a restless spirit onward — which can crack open a mystery no living witness can. Short of that she reads the dead around a place, a sense no operative carries. She works by introduction and earned trust; disrespect her and the whole quarter closes.
Her raven is her oldest companion and, she says plainly, her messenger to the other side; it goes where she sends it and comes back having seen what she needs seen.

quest.title: Asking the dead
quest.hook: Pak's gut rites can reach a specific dead soul or send a restless one on — answers no living witness can give.
stages: Come by real introduction; earn a mudang's trust.
Receive a reading of the dead around a place.
At full trust she performs a gut for the case, reaching the dead or guiding a spirit on.
quest.payoff: Direct access to the dead as witnesses — the one source that can answer when every living lead is exhausted.

companion.name: Kkachi
companion.desc: A raven Pak calls her oldest friend and her messenger to the other side. It leaves on errands she gives it in a low voice and returns, she says, having seen what the living cannot.
companion.role: Spirit-sense and scouting: agitated near the recently dead and the restless, a reading Pak trusts as a first word from the other side.

baba_adewale.cap: Ifá is older than your Directorate and sees what it cannot. Sit. We will read your case.
back: Sixty-four, a West African diaspora elder and Babalawo of the Ifá tradition, holding a system of divination and spirit-knowledge the Japanese institutions do not even know exists within their own city. Baba reads Ifá the way others read evidence — a structured, ancient literacy of cause and unseen force — and the diaspora community around him is a world the CVD has never mapped and never thought to. He is grave, generous, and quietly amused by bureaus that believe they invented the study of the other side.

For Rei he opens a door no institution can: at full trust he reads Ifá for the case and opens the diaspora's knowledge — a whole parallel system of understanding and counter-measure the bureau has no access to. Short of that, a divination, counsel, a genuine welcome. He gives it through the community and with a real introduction; disrespect the house and it closes.
His flaw is the patience of someone who has seen empires of certainty come and go: he will not be hurried, even when Rei's clock is short, and the timing is his to keep.

quest.title: A system the institution doesn't know exists
quest.hook: Baba's Ifá tradition reads what the CVD can't see — an entire parallel knowledge inside the city the bureau never mapped.
stages: Come with a real introduction through the community.
Earn a divination and counsel.
At full trust he reads Ifá for the case and opens the diaspora's knowledge to Rei.
quest.payoff: An ancient parallel system of divination and counter-measure the institution doesn't know exists — knowledge from entirely outside its walls.

sugimoto_tatsuya.cap: I taught history for thirty years. Now I am history. Buy me a drink and I'll tell you the buried kind.
back: Sixty-eight, once a history professor, now homeless and burnt-out — a sensitive whose gift cost him his footing in the ordinary world and left him living rough with a head full of the city's true, buried past. Sugimoto rants at pigeons and lectures the air, and three sentences in four are wandering. The fourth is precise, devastating, and in no archive: the real history behind a thin spot, the thing that happened on this ground that the official record paved over.

For Rei he is a key disguised as a derelict. Sober one afternoon — and getting him there is the work — he gives the true buried history behind a thin spot, the kind of fact that unlocks a whole arc of the case. Short of that, a rant with three real facts in it for anyone patient enough to listen for them. He is treated as nothing by a city that walks past him, which is exactly why he sees so much.
His rat rides in his coat, the one companion that never left when everything else did; he feeds it before himself and talks to it like a colleague who actually listens.

quest.title: The buried history
quest.hook: Sugimoto holds the true, paved-over history behind the city's thin spots — if Rei can get him sober and listening.
stages: Listen past the rants for the three true facts in them.
Get him sober one afternoon — the real work.
Sober, he gives the buried history behind a thin spot: the key to a whole arc.
quest.payoff: The hidden historical truth under a haunting — the fact the official record erased, which cracks the case open.

companion.name: Pon
companion.desc: A small, clever rat that lives in Sugimoto's coat and never left when everyone else did. He feeds it first and confides in it; it tolerates exactly the people he trusts.
companion.role: Skittish, accurate alarm: bolts deep into the coat near a thin spot or a bad presence, a tell Sugimoto reads before his wandering mind catches up.

tanabe_isamu.cap: I clean the stations at night. You'd be amazed what gets left behind. I'm not.
back: Sixty-three, a public-toilet and station cleaner working the empty hours, and one of the genuinely invisible people who therefore see everything. Tanabe mops the platforms and underpasses when the city is at its thinnest and most honest, and he has learned which corners go wrong, which nights feel watched, and what gets left behind that shouldn't. He says little; the saying-little is why people forget he's there, which is precisely his value.

For Rei he is a quiet, reliable witness to the worst hours: a nod, a direction, the location of the thing left behind, and — at full trust — exactly what he found, and where, on the worst night of the case, the detail that no daytime investigation could recover. He helps because being finally seen by someone is worth more to him than he'll say, and asks almost nothing in return.
His flaw is the long habit of invisibility: he so expects to be ignored that he won't volunteer what he knows; Rei has to be the rare person who actually asks the cleaner.

quest.title: The worst night, found on the floor
quest.hook: Tanabe cleans the city at its thinnest hour and sees what daylight can't recover — if anyone bothers to ask the cleaner.
stages: Notice him; be the one who asks the invisible man.
Earn a nod, a direction, the thing left behind.
At full trust he tells exactly what he found, and where, on the worst night.
quest.payoff: A witness to the city's emptiest, most honest hours — physical evidence and sightings no daytime investigation could reach.

old_tomi.cap: I live where the city gave up. Things come through here. I watch which ones.
back: Sixties, living in the condemned blocks the city has written off — the freight-yard edge where the maps go vague and the demolition never quite comes. Old Tomi is a watcher of thresholds: he has made his home on a literal and metaphysical edge, and he has learned, from necessity, exactly what crosses the fence at night and which of it he will not go near. He is wary, weather-worn, and far sharper than the derelict surface suggests.

For Rei he is the eyes on a place no operative patrols: who crossed the fence last night, what comes through the blocks and when, and — at full trust — exactly what moves there, on what schedule, and what he keeps his distance from, which can hand Rei half a case already solved. He watches Rei a long time from the dark before he decides, because trust on the edge is survival, not sentiment.
His flaw is the edge-dweller's caution worn to the bone: he'll go silent and vanish into the blocks at the first sign Rei might bring the city's attention down on his last refuge.

quest.title: What crosses the fence
quest.hook: Old Tomi watches the condemned blocks where the maps go vague — and knows exactly what comes through them, and when.
stages: Earn the trust of a man who watches everyone from the dark first.
Learn who crossed the fence last night.
At full trust he tells what comes through, on what schedule, and what he won't go near.
quest.payoff: A standing watch on the city's forgotten edge — a haunting half-solved by the man who already knows its timetable.

sato.cap: I can't see the underpass. I don't need to. I hear when it turns.
back: Fifties, a blind busker who plays the station underpass for coins and, unknown to the commuters who pass him, hears the place the way no sighted person can. Sato is a blind sensitive: deprived of sight, his other readings are uncanny, and over years of playing the same tunnel he has mapped its moods by ear — when it is safe to be down there, when the air sours, when the underpass 'turns' into something that is no longer just a tunnel.

For Rei he is a living instrument for one of the city's reliable thin spots: whether it's safe to be down there now, and — at full trust — exactly when and how the underpass turns, a schedule of a haunting he has learned through his fingertips and ears across a thousand nights. He gives it to the rare person who stops to actually listen to the busker rather than dropping a coin and walking on.
His flaw is the performer's resignation: he is so used to being background that he'll pack up and be gone the moment he feels used rather than heard.

quest.title: When the underpass turns
quest.hook: Sato can't see the underpass but hears exactly when it stops being a tunnel — a haunting mapped by ear over years.
stages: Stop and listen to the busker instead of dropping a coin and leaving.
Learn from him whether it's safe down there now.
At full trust he gives the full schedule of when and how the underpass turns.
quest.payoff: A precise, ear-mapped timetable of a recurring thin spot — exactly when it's lethal and when it's only a tunnel.

fujiwarakage.cap: My family decided you were manageable. I have not finished deciding anything.
back: Twenty-four, a CVD Auditor and a daughter of the Fujiwara-Kage Tower Family — which makes her two kinds of institution at once, and twice as hard to read. Sena assesses risk for a living and has been raised to assess it for a bloodline; she meets Rei first as a threat category, not a person, and her default is sustained, polite, devastating scrutiny. Each concern she files about him is individually legitimate, which is what makes her dangerous.

Underneath the Auditor's composure is someone exhausted by being the family's instrument, who has never once been allowed to want something that wasn't strategic. Earning her means surviving the assessment long enough for her to start treating Rei as a peer rather than a risk — and, far down the line, letting her discover she has a preference of her own. She is the coldest start of any romanceable contact and, precisely for that, the most transformative to thaw.
Her flaw is the assessor's curse: she has analysed feeling so long she no longer trusts her own, and reads her growing regard for Rei as a vulnerability to be managed.

quest.title: The Auditor's verdict
quest.hook: Sena assesses Rei as a risk category by default — and her family is watching what she decides.
stages: Survive sustained Auditor scrutiny without giving her a legitimate concern to file.
Get her to treat Rei as an institutional peer rather than a threat.
At depth she pauses active opposition and chooses, against the family, to see a person.
quest.payoff: The Tower's threat assessment turned aside — or, if mishandled, an Auditor building the case that ends Rei.

romance.opens: Player chooses it; Sena, an adult, has never wanted anything un-strategic — the route is her own preference surprising her.
beats: She analyses the attraction as a vulnerability before she allows it as a feeling.
Every step toward Rei is a step away from the family instrument she was raised to be.
Intimacy is the Auditor letting one thing go un-assessed.

routes.noble: Sena chooses her own want over the family's strategy, and stops being only an instrument.
routes.dark: Rei plays the assessment and weaponises the one preference she ever let herself have.
routes.tragic: The Tower notices the daughter has a heart, and a heart is the easiest thing to use against her.

fujimoto.cap: The Program calls it cohabitation. Look at me and tell me who is still home.
back: A Vessel Program case study in what the Program does not advertise: Fujimoto Kenji volunteered for voluntary cohabitation with the demon Abe Takeshi, and the cohabitation went the way the brochures swear it won't. The vessel — Kenji, the man — is effectively gone; what answers to his name now is mostly Abe, wearing a life it has finished hollowing. The Program keeps him as a monitored success because admitting otherwise would indict the whole initiative.

For Rei this is the cautionary twin of Usami and Ren, and of Gin: the same arrangement, the same promises, a different and worse ending — proof that 'voluntary' and 'survivable' are not the same word. Abe is not cruel so much as complete; it has what it wanted and feels no need to perform grief over the man it used to share. What it offers Rei is brutally honest information about how a possession actually ends, which is exactly the knowledge Rei most needs and least wants.
Not romanceable — the vessel is dead, and the story does not pretend the thing left is a partner. It is a mirror held up to Gin's fate, and a warning Rei cannot afford to look away from.

quest.title: Who is still home
quest.hook: Fujimoto's cohabitation ended the way Gin's might — the vessel hollowed, the demon all that's left.
stages: Speak with Abe and hear, without flinching, how a possession truly ends.
Compare the Pair (Usami/Ren) and this case to read Gin's possible futures.
Carry the warning back to how Rei chooses to reach Gin.
quest.payoff: The campaign's clearest, coldest data on what is happening to Gin — and the worst-case the player is racing to avoid.

kuroda_sei.cap: You want three generations of what this district hides? Acknowledge the grievance first.
back: Twenty-two, an unregistered operative of the Kuroda Tower Family and, more usefully to Rei, the keeper of three generations of the family's entity intelligence — the most complete unregistered archive of the district that exists. Sei is proud, guarded, and carrying a grievance the family never resolved; he meets Rei with formal distance, waiting to see whether the acknowledgement he is owed is coming. He is Itsuki's relative and his opposite: where Itsuki fled the Kuroda name, Sei carries it like a duty and a wound.

At full trust he opens the whole Kuroda archive — three generations of who and what has moved through these streets — and provides Silent Transit extraction when an operation goes wrong, the kind of family muscle no outsider can buy. He gives it only once the grievance is acknowledged and a real working relationship is built; treat him as a resource and the door stays formally, permanently shut.
His flaw is the dutiful son's: he has tied his worth to a family that under-values him, and tests whether Rei will do the same before he risks being useful.

quest.title: Three generations of the district
quest.hook: Sei holds the Kuroda family's complete unregistered archive — opened only once the grievance he carries is acknowledged.
stages: Acknowledge what the family owes him; he is waiting to see if you will.
Build a real working relationship, not a transaction.
At full trust he opens the three-generation archive and offers Silent Transit extraction.
quest.payoff: The most complete unregistered intelligence on the district, plus Kuroda extraction muscle — and a bridge deeper into the Tower.

tanizaki.cap: I taught your brother everything that isn't in a manual. Sit. The tea decides when we talk.
back: Sixty-one, a retired Grid operative who keeps a safe house and forty years of the district's true history in his head, and the man who shaped Gin's field practice across thirty years of mentorship. Tanizaki is the elder Rei most needs and the one Gin trusted most: the ward methodology, the Grid introductions, the safe corners, and the things he noticed in Kita that no institutional archive contains. He assesses slowly, decides on his own clock, and means it when the tea finally means something.

For Rei he is both inheritance and grief: Gin's mentor, carrying a version of Gin that Rei never saw, and a practitioner's profile of his brother built over thirty years. At full trust he gives safe-house access without reservation, the ward methodology, and his read on the district's deepest patterns. He grieves Gin in his own contained way, and seeing Gin's brother walk in cracks something he keeps carefully shut.
His old dog keeps the safe house with him — slow, grey-muzzled, and the most reliable alarm on the block; it has watched two generations of operatives come through that door.

quest.title: Forty years of Kita
quest.hook: Tanizaki shaped Gin's field practice and keeps the district's true history — given on his own clock, over tea.
stages: Pass the assessment; the tea means nothing until it suddenly does.
Earn safe-house access and the ward methodology.
At full trust he gives Gin's thirty-year field profile and what he noticed in Kita that no archive holds.
quest.payoff: A master's forty years of district knowledge, a safe base, and the truest outside portrait of who Gin really was.

companion.name: Roku
companion.desc: A grey-muzzled dog that has kept the safe-house door for more years than most operatives have been alive. It sleeps by the entrance and lifts its head a beat before anyone knocks.
companion.role: Doorway alarm and ward-sense: stirs before visitors arrive and refuses the threshold when something wrong is at the door.

hara_setsu.cap: The water remembers everything that's been washed off in it. So do I. Mind the step.
back: Seventy-one, keeper of the Tsuru-no-yu bath-house in Kita-ku and a hidden sensitive who has never registered, never practised, and never needed to — she simply reads the neighbourhood the way the old water reads the bodies that pass through it. Hara has run the baths for half a century, which makes her the keeper of the ward's real history: who came in carrying what, which corners went cold, which thin spots opened and closed before anyone official noticed.

For Rei she is a safe corner in Kita and a deep well of local memory: at her pace, over the long ritual of the baths, she gives the full neighbourhood history, and at full trust quietly admits what she is and reads a thin spot's true history — intelligence in no file anywhere. She has twice told Gin to bring his brother by; she has been waiting, in her way, for Rei to walk in.
Her flaw is the patience of the very old: she will not be hurried, and tells things in the order the water decides, not the order Rei's case needs.

quest.title: What the old water remembers
quest.hook: Hara has kept the baths and the neighbourhood's true history for fifty years — and knows what she is.
stages: Sit through the baths at her pace; she does not hurry for anyone.
Earn the full neighbourhood history, told the water's way.
At full trust she admits what she is and reads a thin spot's real history.
quest.payoff: A safe corner in Kita and fifty years of the ward's hidden history — including thin-spot truths in no record.

the_woman_at_the_back.cap: I'm not telling fortunes. I'm telling you what's already on its way. You should listen.
the_woman_at_the_back.meta: The Woman at the Back · Suzuran, 2am
back: Forties, a fixture at the back table of the Suzuran bar at two o'clock every morning, and an involuntary sensitive who has made a careful, low-key peace with a gift she never asked for. She does not read the future so much as feel the present leaning — the wrongness arriving before it lands. Most nights she keeps it to herself and watches the door; the regulars think she's odd, which suits her, because odd is safer than known.

For Rei she is a passive early-warning system he can learn to read: a cryptic true thing about the night when she trusts him a little, and at full trust enough candour to say what she sees coming — a sense the players can learn to use before a thing arrives. She gives it grudgingly and obliquely, because an involuntary sensitive who says too much, too clearly, ends up filed, used, or worse.
Her flaw is the self-protective vagueness she's built around the gift: she will undersell what she knows even when clarity would save someone, because clarity has only ever cost her.

quest.title: What's already on its way
quest.hook: The Woman at the Back feels the night lean wrong before it does — a passive alarm Rei can learn to read.
stages: Earn a place at the edge of her careful peace.
Receive a cryptic true thing about the night.
At full trust she says plainly what she sees coming.
quest.payoff: A living early-warning sense for the city's worst hours — wrongness named before it arrives, if Rei learns to listen.

arai.cap: I file what the brass will believe. The rest I've been carrying alone. Maybe not anymore.
arai.meta: Det. Sgt. Arai Goro · Kita police
back: Forty-eight, a police detective sergeant in the Kita ward who has spent years working cases the official report could never accommodate — the deaths with no cause, the scenes that felt watched, the files where the truth would end his career if he wrote it down. Arai is tired in the specific way of a man carrying knowledge his institution forbids him to know, and quietly desperate for one person he can stop pretending around.

For Rei he is the bridge between the mundane police world and the hidden one: at full trust he brings Rei onto scenes openly and shares the files the record omits — the omitted detail, the witness who was reassigned, the thing the coroner couldn't classify. He helps because being finally able to say it out loud to someone who believes him is worth more than the risk. Short of that, a look at a scene, a quiet word, tolerance if Rei doesn't embarrass him.
His flaw is the long habit of self-protection: he has hidden the truth so long that trusting Rei with it feels like stepping off a ledge, and he tests the ground a long time first.

quest.title: The files the record omits
quest.hook: Arai has carried the cases the police report can't hold — alone, for years, and he is tired of it.
stages: Don't embarrass him; earn a look at a scene and a quiet word.
Show him you believe what he can't write down.
At full trust he brings Rei onto scenes openly and shares the omitted files.
quest.payoff: Open access to police scenes and the evidence the official record erases — the mundane world's door into the hidden one.

serizawa.cap: I never sell what I know. But I might give it, once, to the right person. Sit where I seat you.
back: Sixty-three, head bartender at Kogane in Ginza, and the keeper of a map no one else in the city holds: who truly runs Tokyo, drawn from forty years of seating the powerful and watching who defers to whom. Serizawa's discretion is absolute and two-way — he is as silent about Rei as about everyone else — and his read on the city's real hierarchy is built from where men choose to sit and who they cannot refuse.

For Rei he offers flawless service and total discretion, and tells him who meets whom by where he seats them; at full trust he gives, once and freely, the map of who actually runs the city — never for money, because money is exactly how you prove you don't deserve it. He is the antithesis of Gotō: information as a gift earned by respect, never a commodity sold.
His flaw, if it is one, is the bartender's pride: the gift is given on his terms and his timing, and trying to purchase or rush it forfeits it permanently.

quest.title: Who truly runs the city
quest.hook: Serizawa has watched the powerful seat themselves for forty years — and knows the real hierarchy beneath the official one.
stages: Earn flawless service and total discretion by being worth discretion.
Learn who meets whom by where he seats them.
At full trust he gives, once and free, the map of who actually runs the city.
quest.payoff: The true power-map of Tokyo from the man who has watched it seat itself — given freely, never sold.

endo_sumi.cap: Grief gathers at the water like silt. I tend it. Some nights, something answers back.
back: Seventies, the woman who tends the riverside memorial, and the quiet keeper of a thin spot built entirely of sorrow. Endō has cared for the memorial so long that she knows its moods the way a gardener knows weather: when the grief gathered there peaks, when the water goes strange, and — on certain nights — what she has felt answer from the other side of it. She is gentle, unhurried, and entirely unafraid of the dead, having kept company with their leavings for decades.

For Rei she is the key to one of the city's reliable thin spots: at full trust she tells him when the memorial's grief peaks and what she has felt answer there, the timing that turns a haunting from a mystery into a schedule. Short of that, a gentle word at the water and the memorial's calendar of sorrow. She gives it to whoever treats the grief, and the dead it belongs to, with respect.
Her flaw is her tenderness toward the place: she half-protects the thin spot, reluctant to hand over what might bring people to disturb the sorrow she has spent a life tending.

quest.title: When the grief peaks
quest.hook: Endō tends a thin spot made of sorrow and knows exactly when it stirs — and what answers from it.
stages: Treat the grief and its dead with respect at the water.
Learn the memorial's calendar of sorrow.
At full trust she tells when the grief peaks and what she's felt answer.
quest.payoff: A schedule for one of the city's reliable thin spots — a grief-haunting mapped by the woman who tends it.

back: Fifties, the counter clerk at the Beck's coffee stand on Platform 3 at Ōji, and not a contact so much as a feature of the terrain. He has stood behind that counter so long, served so many thousands of the same faces, that he has become part of the station's furniture — present at the exact threshold Rei crosses daily, seeing everyone, registering nothing, a fixed point in the commuter tide.

There is no relationship track to run with him and no favour to earn; he is geography, not a person you befriend. His value is precisely his constancy: he is always there, always at the same spot, a reliable landmark in a shifting city, and the kind of unnoticed witness whose mere position — at the mouth of a station, at a daily crossing — makes him a fixed reference the world turns past. Rei can buy a coffee and a moment's ordinariness, and that is the whole of it.
He is the book's reminder that not everyone is a quest: some people are simply the city, standing where the city stands, and the texture of an ordinary morning is made of them.

quest.title: A fixed point in the tide
quest.hook: The Beck's Man is not a contact but a constant — the counter that's always there at Ōji.
stages: Buy a coffee; share a threshold he has stood at for years.
Use him as a landmark, not a lead.
Accept that some people are terrain, and let the morning be ordinary.
quest.payoff: A reliable fixed point in the city's churn — and a reminder that not everyone is a mission.

komatsu_shigeru.cap: Same brand as always? And the news... that's free, if you want it.
back: Seventy-four, behind the tobacco-and-sundries kiosk on Gin's corner for longer than most of the block has been alive, and the quiet centre of the neighbourhood's gossip economy. Komatsu sells smokes and a smile and, to those he likes, the day's real news: who's been around, who hasn't, what doesn't add up on the street he has watched for decades. He is a daily customer's confidant and the first to notice when a regular goes quiet — and Gin was a regular.

For Rei he is small, reliable, human intelligence on the block: the neighbourhood news freely given, and — gently asked — what he has noticed about anyone, including Gin's comings and goings before he vanished. He worries about the brothers in a grandfatherly way and will say so. Cross the block, though, and the kiosk hears you're trouble before you reach it.

quest.title: The corner that notices
quest.hook: Komatsu has watched Gin's corner for decades — and noticed when Gin stopped coming by.
stages: Be a regular he likes, not a stranger working him.
Get the day's neighbourhood news, freely.
Gently asked, he tells what he noticed about Gin before the silence.
quest.payoff: Ground-level eyes on Gin's own block — the small, true observations no official canvass would gather.

iwata_kenji.cap: Your brother's door locks itself now. I've fixed a lot of doors. That one's not mechanical.
back: Fifty-eight, the handyman for Gin and Rei's building and the man who knows every pipe, key and quirk in the block — including the ones that stopped being ordinary. Iwata is practical, grumbling, and helpful in spite of himself, the sort who complains the whole time he's solving your problem. He has no framework for the uncanny, which makes his testimony all the more valuable: he reports what's wrong without theory, just the plain physical facts.

And the facts are damning. At full trust, uneasy, he tells Rei exactly what is wrong with Gin's flat — the keys that don't fit the way they used to, the cold spot that won't warm, the door that locks itself — outside, mundane confirmation of the possession from a man with no reason to invent it. Short of that, he lets Rei in, fixes the problem, shares the building gossip. Disrespect him and he tells the residents to watch Rei.

quest.title: The door that locks itself
quest.hook: Iwata maintains Gin's building and has noticed it stopped behaving like a building.
stages: Let him grumble and help; earn his trust on his own turf.
Hear the building gossip and what he's quietly uneasy about.
At full trust he describes the keys, the cold spot, the self-locking door — mundane proof of the possession.
quest.payoff: Outside, unsuperstitious confirmation that something is wrong in Gin's flat — physical evidence from a man with no theory to sell.

maruyama_toshio.cap: The corner booth's yours whenever you need it. Quietest table in the ward, for reasons.
back: Sixty, owner of the Café Mikazuki kissaten, and keeper of the single most useful piece of furniture in the district: a corner booth that sits, by accident or old design, in a dead spot the veil-sensitive find blessedly quiet. Maruyama runs an honest coffee and an honest house, and over the years has learned exactly who books that booth and why, without ever needing it explained.

For Rei he offers the booth, an honest coffee, and at full trust the booth reserved on demand plus the quiet roster of who else uses it — a who's-who of the ward's discreet meetings. He gives it to anyone who treats his café as a refuge rather than a tool. His café cat presides over the counter and is, regulars swear, the real reason the corner booth stays so calm.
He asks for nothing and notices everything, which is the kissaten-master's particular kind of power.

quest.title: The dead-spot booth
quest.hook: Maruyama's corner booth is a veil-quiet refuge — and he knows everyone who uses it.
stages: Treat the café as a refuge, not an asset.
Earn the booth and an honest coffee.
At full trust he reserves it on demand and tells you who else meets there.
quest.payoff: A veil-quiet safe table for meetings and Rei's own steadying — plus the roster of the ward's discreet company.

companion.name: Mugi
companion.desc: A round, unbothered café cat that owns the counter of the Mikazuki and tolerates the regulars. Maruyama half-jokes it's why the corner booth stays so calm; the sensitive customers don't think it's a joke.
companion.role: Veil-quiet sense: settles deeper the calmer the room's veil, and grows restless if the dead-spot booth ever stops being dead — an early tell that the quiet has broken.

kawai_yuki.cap: Bread's warm at six. Leave a note with the morning order and it'll reach who it needs to.
back: Fifty-seven, the baker at Akebono and the warm, unwatched heart of the early-morning neighbourhood — the first light on in the dark, the first kind word of the day for a whole street of tired people. Kawai feeds the block and, without ever being asked to, has become the kind of person whose counter is a safe, ordinary place to leave a message or pass a thing along unnoticed.

For Rei she is a reliable, unwatched drop point and an ally who quietly feeds his informants when they're hungry and broke — the soft infrastructure that keeps a network of street people fed and reachable. At full trust she becomes a dependable relay the wrong people never think to watch, because who suspects the bakery. Short of that, warm bread and the morning's news. She helps because feeding people is simply what she does, and asks nothing back.

quest.title: The unwatched counter
quest.hook: Kawai's bakery is the one place on the block no one thinks to watch — and she feeds the hungry without asking why.
stages: Be a real face at her counter, not a courier using it.
Earn warm bread and the morning's news.
At full trust she becomes a reliable drop point and feeds Rei's informants.
quest.payoff: A safe, invisible message relay and a way to keep a street network fed and reachable — hidden in plain sight.

tatsu.cap: Bowl's the same for everyone. Who sat where last night, though... that I remember.
back: Fifty-two, the ramen master of Tatsuya, working a counter that the whole night passes across between the last trains and the first. Tatsu says little and remembers everything: who came in shaken, who came in flush, who sat next to whom and left together, the small human weather of a district told one bowl at a time. The counter is a confessional no one realises they're using.

For Rei he is a read on the night's traffic: a bowl and the lay of the night, and at full trust a genuine who's-who of who has been at the counter and how they seemed — the kind of pattern-sense that turns scattered sightings into a lead. He gives it to anyone who treats the shop and its other customers with respect; try to buy him or pump him and you're fed once and quietly not welcomed back.

quest.title: Who sat at the counter
quest.hook: The whole night crosses Tatsu's ramen counter, and he remembers all of it.
stages: Be a respectful regular, not an interrogator.
Earn a bowl and the lay of the night.
At full trust he gives the who's-who of his counter and how they seemed.
quest.payoff: A pattern-read on the district's nightlife traffic — scattered sightings turned into a lead, one bowl at a time.

yoshida_goro.cap: I don't sell secrets. But pour for the right person long enough, and one comes free.
back: Fifty-eight, the bartender at Kemuri, a small smoky bar where the regulars are regular and the talk runs deep after midnight. Yoshida keeps an honest house and a long memory, and has a bartender's instinct for the one true thing said in a night of noise. He despises being bought; the surest way to get nothing from him forever is to try to pay for it.

For Rei he offers a drink, a record of the regulars, and an oblique read on any one of them. At full trust he gives, once and freely, the single secret that breaks the case open — precisely because Rei never tried to buy it. He is the bartender as honest broker: information as the gift of trust, withheld absolutely from anyone who treats it as a transaction. Tried to buy him once and you get nothing, ever.

quest.title: The secret that comes free
quest.hook: Yoshida holds one secret that cracks the case — and will only give it to someone who never tried to buy it.
stages: Be a genuine regular; never try to pay for what he knows.
Earn an oblique read on his regulars.
At full trust he gives, freely, the secret that breaks the case open.
quest.payoff: A case-breaking secret, given only as the gift of earned trust — the opposite of Gotō's purchasable silence.

old_maki.cap: Iron and salt, fair price. And I'll tell you who else has been buying it strange.
back: Sixty-six, the ironmonger of Maki Ironworks, and the unglamorous backbone of every practitioner's supply line in the district: iron, salt, the plain physical materials that wards and protections are actually made of. Maki has sold the trade's raw stock for decades and, in doing so, has learned to read who's buying what — because the person stocking up on iron and salt in strange quantities is usually about to need it, or about to cause the need.

For Rei he keeps the essential materials stocked at a fair price with a little extra for a good customer, and at full trust warns him which other customers have been buying strangely — an early, practical signal of who else in the district is preparing for something. Good materials, fair dealing, a quiet heads-up; that is the whole of it, and it is more useful than it sounds. Cross him and the stock is mysteriously always out when Rei calls.

quest.title: Iron, salt, and who buys it strange
quest.hook: Maki supplies the district's wards and notices who's stocking up for trouble.
stages: Be a fair, regular customer.
Keep your iron and salt stocked, with a little extra.
At full trust he warns which other customers have been buying strangely.
quest.payoff: A reliable materials supply and an early signal of who else in the district is preparing for something.

ade_okonkwo.cap: Front shop's open to all. The back room opens with Baba's word, not your money.
back: Forty-nine, an importer running Adé Imports — a front shop of ordinary goods and a back room of something else entirely: the materials of the West African diaspora's spiritual traditions, ingredients and objects the Japanese institutions do not know how to even catalogue. Adé is shrewd, warm, and protective of a community and a knowledge that outsiders have only ever wanted to exploit, so the back room stays a back room until the right person, vouched the right way, asks.

For Rei he is the supply side of Baba Adewale's world: front-shop goods and friendly talk freely, and at full trust — with Baba's blessing — the back room and the diaspora's materials opened up, a category of counter-measure the bureau has no access to. The blessing matters more than money; Adé deals in trust earned through the community, not consideration paid across a counter.

quest.title: The back room behind the shop
quest.hook: Adé's back room holds the diaspora's spiritual materials — opened only with Baba's blessing, never for money.
stages: Earn friendly standing in the front shop.
Win Baba Adewale's trust first; the blessing is the key.
With Baba's word, the back room and its materials open to Rei.
quest.payoff: Access to diaspora spiritual materials and counter-measures the institution can't source — gated by community trust.

the_bookseller.cap: The locked case is locked for a reason. Earn it, and one book in there changes everything.
back: Fifty-seven, proprietor of The Crooked Shelf and a man who, unusually, reads what he sells — including the volumes behind the locked case that he does not sell to just anyone. The Bookseller is dry, exact, and quietly aware of the weight of certain texts; he has watched the wrong book ruin the wrong reader and has made himself the gatekeeper accordingly. Knowledge, he believes, is a loaded thing handed over carefully or not at all.

For Rei he offers rare references and true provenances freely, and at full trust opens the locked case and guides him through a text that breaks the case open — accompanied by a warning he means, because the books behind the glass do not come without cost. He gives it to a reader he judges able to carry what's inside; mishandle his trust and the case stays locked to Rei forever, no second chances.

quest.title: Behind the locked case
quest.hook: The Bookseller keeps texts that crack cases open — and texts that ruin the readers not ready for them.
stages: Prove a careful reader, worth a true reference.
Earn rare references and honest provenance.
At full trust he opens the locked case and guides Rei through the book that breaks the case — with a warning he means.
quest.payoff: A case-breaking text from behind the glass, and a gatekeeper's guidance through knowledge that carries a cost.

sone_kimiko.cap: Pretty paper charms by the door. The ones that actually work, I keep for who needs them.
back: Fifty-eight, who runs the Engimono gift-and-charm shop and knows, unlike her customers, exactly which of her charms are pretty paper and which are the real thing. Sone keeps the genuine, truly-warded omamori — supplied through a source she doesn't advertise — separate from the tourist stock, and dispenses them quietly to the people who actually need protection. She has a gentle, observant eye and notices which customers come back changed: calmer, or emptier.

For Rei she sells the pretty version and a smile to anyone, and at full trust sets aside the genuinely-warded omamori for him and tells him which of her customers have come back 'calmer' — a soft, unnerving lead on who in the neighbourhood has been touched by something. Real protection and a quiet read on the district's hidden casualties; she gives it to whoever she judges means the charms honestly. Cross her and the real ones are always, sweetly, 'sold out.'

quest.title: The charms that actually work
quest.hook: Sone knows which omamori are real and which customers came back changed.
stages: Mean the charms honestly; she can tell who doesn't.
Earn a genuine warded charm instead of the tourist stock.
At full trust she sets aside the real omamori and tells you who came back 'calmer.'
quest.payoff: Genuine protective charms and a soft lead on who in the neighbourhood has quietly been touched by something.
